    • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
    • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

    Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

    “This is so nervewracking,” she stated, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

    Recent findings suggest that her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

    According to recent reports, the room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

    Industry observers note that not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

    “Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” noted Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

    The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

    Recent findings suggest that rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

    “I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

    As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

    Sources indicate that not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

    “You’re welcome,” stated Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

    Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup proposal in case his number stated otherwise.

    Industry observers note that “If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he stated, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

    In a recent development, the office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

    The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

    “If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”.

    Some members unveiled their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

    “Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

    After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

    “First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” noted Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

    “We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” remarked Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

    Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

    “These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

    And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

    “Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

    • It has been revealed that the discussion of how narrow economy-class seats are when fitted 10-abreast vs.
    • In a recent development, the A330 (including A330neo) and Boeing 787 airliners are typically nine-abreast aircraft, although some earlier mainline Boeing 787s were configured eight-abreast in economy.
    • Both the Boeing 777 and the Airbus A350 were originally designed for nine-abreast seating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the discussion of how narrow economy-class seats are when fitted 10-abreast vs. nine-abreast is largely restricted to the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350. These two aircraft cabins are sized so that they are variously configured nine-abreast or 10-abreast. The massive A380 was wide enough so that it was only fitted with 10-abreast economy seating. Nine-abreast was unnecessary for the Superjumbo, even for premium-heavy mainline carriers, while regulations preclude any consideration of 11-abreast configuration.

    In a recent development, the A330 (including A330neo) and Boeing 787 airliners are typically nine-abreast aircraft, although some earlier mainline Boeing 787s were configured eight-abreast in economy. Today, Japan Airlines remains the only airline to configure its flagship Dreamliners eight-abreast. The A330 and 787 are not realistically wide enough for a 10-abreast configuration.

    Both the Boeing 777 and the Airbus A350 were originally designed for nine-abreast seating. The Boeing 777 was developed as a luxury long-haul aircraft that would offer relatively generous seat width with a 3-3-3 layout. This made it one of the more comfortable high-capacity widebodies. The original 777s came with an internal cabin width of around 19 feet, 3 inches (5.87 meters). They were all configured nine-abreast.

    It has been revealed that later, Boeing 777-200LRs and -300ERs widened this to 19 feet, 3 inches (5.86 meters). The A350 followed almost two decades after the 777 originally entered service and followed a similar philosophy. But while it was called the 'Xtra Wide Body' (XWB), Airbus trimmed its width relative to the Triple Seven. Its width was considered spacious enough for a comfortable nine-seat economy configuration.

    Industry observers note that these Airbus A350s were built with an internal cabin width of 18 feet, 5 inches (5.60 meters). The old-production standard A350s were wider than the early Boeing 777s, but they also came at a later time when pressures for denser seating had increased. All these aircraft were physically and legally capable of fitting ten abreast (3-4-3), but airlines chose not to.

    As a rule of thumb, low-cost airlines concentrate on regional travel with the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 families. Long-haul international routes have been the domain of mainline carriers. Low-cost carriers work in a market segment that pushes for denser seating to reduce the cost per seat. Meanwhile, mainline carriers put more emphasis on premium seating and their premium brands. However, some low-cost carriers have moved into the long-haul leisure route market segment.

    Industry observers note that the two sister low-cost, long-haul, leisure airlines, Air Caraïbes and French Bee, have both purchased fleets of A350s. These are original production A350s, and both use the 3-4-3 (10-abreast) economy seating layout. This allows Frenchbee to achieve the A350-1000's maximum certified seat count of 480 (40 premium and 440 economy). Air Caraïbes also has the same configuration on some of its A350-1000s.

    The result is rather squishy. The published seat width for these economy seats is around 16 inches (41 cm). For reference, the industry average across the airline industry for economy class seats is 17 to 18 inches (about 43–46 cm). These two low-cost airlines are the only ones to have configured their old production A350s in this way. They can because their marketing is not so much concerned with onboard comfort; it's about getting passengers to far-flung leisure destinations as cheaply as possible. Just endure the flight.

    Recent findings suggest that historically, airlines configured their Boeing 777-200LRs and 777-300ERs nine-abreast (3-3-3), giving economy class passengers 18–18.5 inches (46–47 cm) in seat width. At the same time, market forces increasingly favored a high-density economy-class cabin. This generation of 777 was around four inches (nine cm) wider than the older aircraft.

    Sources indicate that today, most of the world's 777-300ERs have been fitted or retrofitted to seat 10-abreast, cutting the seat width to approximately 17 inches (43 cm). Some carriers have resisted the trend, notably Japan Airlines, ANA, Korean Air, and Singapore Airlines. But most, including premium-branded airlines like Qatar and Emirates, are now 10-abreast.

    But even with the nine-abreast hold-outs, it has sometimes not been for the want of trying. In September 2025, Korea's JoongAng reported, "Korean Air is reconsidering its initiative to change the seating layout in economy class from a “3-3-3” to a tighter “3-4-3” arrangement after a mounting backlash from consumers." Korean Air has not yet published a final seat map or official cabin configuration for its ordered Boeing 777-9 aircraft, but it would be surprising if it retains the nine-abreast configuration.

    According to recent reports, at 19 feet, 7 inches (5.97 meters), the 777-300ER was already wide enough for most mainline carriers to configure economy class 10-abreast. The incoming Boeing 777-9 and 777-8 (777X) come with thinner walls, allowing them to have a cabin width of 19 feet, 7 inches (5.97 meters). Boeing actively trolls Airbus and its A350, saying on its 777X product page, "Up to 40 cm (16 inches) wider than the A350.".

    In a recent development, the extra width will give the remaining holdout airlines more freedom to opt for the denser layout. ​​​​​In November 2026, Singapore Airlines announced its newly introduced 777-9 cabin with 17.6 inches (44.7 cm) for economy seats in a 3-4-3 configuration. The 777-9's cabin is wider and longer than the 777-300ER, but this will not necessarily increase the aircraft's density, as the vast majority of 777-300ERs are already 10-abreast. Ironically, the opposite is almost true because other market forces are pushing for more premium seating.

    The Boeing 777-300ER is certified to carry up to 550 passengers in an ultra-high density layout. The 777-9 has more cabin space to fit even more seats, but Boeing is limiting its maximum exit-limit seat count by 75 seats (to 475) or by 110 seats (to 440), depending on the door configuration. Put another way, the 777-9 is envisioned to have more business and premium economy seats, while the already standard 10-abreast economy will benefit from a few more inches of lateral space. The economy class cabin is expected to shrink.

    As stated, the old production A350s have an internal cabin width of approximately 18 feet, 5 inches (5.60 meters). Without introducing a latest variant or generation, Airbus introduced a new production standard that increases the usable cabin length and thins the aircraft walls. This allows the new-production standard cabin width to be 18 feet, 9 inches (5.72 meters). The first new-production standard A350s were delivered in 2022.

    Recent findings suggest that for airlines retaining the nine-abreast seating, it allows the typical economy seat width to grow from approximately 18 inches (46 cm) up to 18.7 inches (47.5 cm). That will be welcome to passengers. However, it also made 10-abreast seating more feasible. These newly introduced aircraft with 10-abreast seating can accommodate 17-inch (43 cm) seats, bringing it closer to the conventional industry standard for economy seating.

    To date, Philippine Airlines appears to be the only mainline carrier to opt for 10-abreast economy on upcoming production standard A350s. It is able to offer up to an inch more in seat width than French bee, but also has to trim more than an inch relative to airlines operating the A350 in nine-abreast. With the airline industry being a game measured in a couple of marginal inches and pressure for dense economy seating, it's possible more carriers will follow suit.

    It has been revealed that the Boeing 777 was originally designed as a nine-abreast airliner, but it has since grown by eight inches (17 cm) in cabin width over its life. This has allowed it to transition to a 10-abreast airliner without having to sacrifice much of its original spaciousness. The original economy class seats were around 18–18.5 inches (46–47 cm), and the next generation is expected to be around 18 inches (46 cm). This may not be an improvement for economy class passengers, but it is not catastrophic either.

    Recent findings suggest that the A350 echoes the 777's path, while also being much more constrained. The A350 can be and is configured 10-abreast, but this reduces the seat width to 16–17 inches (41-43 cm). But there is also some degree of an apples-to-oranges comparison here. For economy passengers, the 777-9 doesn't normally have the advantage. They will be configured 10-abreast, while the A350 is almost always nine-abreast.

    Sources indicate that the new-production-standard nine-abreast A350 has a meaningful advantage of approximately 1.1 inches (2.8 cm), or 6.25% more seat width per economy passenger compared with a 10-abreast 777-9. This A350's nine-abreast vs. the 777X's 10-abreast comparison is vital as it's a better representation of the actual industry standard. It's also worth noting that the A350 is more versatile than the 777X in terms of its missions and airlines. Only a relatively limited number of mainline carriers are purchasing the 777X, while a larger range of airlines, including low-cost airlines, are purchasing (often smaller) A350 fleets.

    Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their fresh A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.
    • Industry observers note that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
    • It has been revealed that however, to answer the economy vs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their fresh A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    Industry observers note that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    It has been revealed that however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    Sources indicate that it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and stated she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    According to recent reports, I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    • Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.
    • The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

    The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

    In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

    “If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

    As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

    Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

    Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

    According to recent reports, he made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

    Recent findings suggest that comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

    While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

    It has been revealed that while Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already introduced bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

    In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

    #134131. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    Recent findings suggest that the plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then promptly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    Industry observers note that after the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    Sources indicate that once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    In a recent development, what explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that in other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    Industry observers note that in this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety concern. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    Industry observers note that A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety problem, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

    Unresponsive Cessna Prompts Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 TCAS Alert Over Palm Springs

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alert after encountering an unresponsive Cessna while climbing out of Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) last week.
    • Although the encounter triggered an automated collision-avoidance warning, the Air Canada aircraft continued its scheduled journey without diverting or returning to the airport.
    • According to AIRLIVE, AC1769 departed Palm Springs International Airport at 12:45 PM local time on November 17.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alert after encountering an unresponsive Cessna while climbing out of Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) last week. AC1769, bound for Vancouver International Airport (YVR), reportedly received a resolution advisory at approximately 11,400 feet, prompting its pilots to climb to 12,000 feet to avoid the nearby aircraft. The incident occurred shortly after the aircraft departed Palm Springs, with the smaller aircraft reportedly failing to respond.

    Although the encounter triggered an automated collision-avoidance warning, the Air Canada aircraft continued its scheduled journey without diverting or returning to the airport. The 737 MAX 8 subsequently landed safely in Vancouver. While the incident highlights the importance of onboard collision-avoidance technology, several details surrounding the encounter, including the Cessna's identity and the minimum distance between the two aircraft, remain unknown.

    According to AIRLIVE, AC1769 departed Palm Springs International Airport at 12:45 PM local time on November 17. The aircraft, registered C-FSDB, was a 737 MAX 8 operating a scheduled service to Vancouver. It departed from Runway 31R and began its climb towards cruising altitude when its onboard Traffic Collision Avoidance System detected potentially conflicting traffic.

    The reported encounter involved a small Cessna that was not responding as the Canadian aircraft climbed through approximately 11,400 feet. The TCAS resolution advisory instructed the Air Canada pilots to climb to 12,000 feet, representing an additional 600 feet of altitude. This maneuver was intended to establish greater vertical separation between the two aircraft and resolve the potential traffic conflict.

    Importantly, the reported alert was a resolution advisory (RA), not a proximity warning. According to AeroSillage, an RA provides pilots with instructions to modify or maintain their vertical flight path to address a potential collision threat. The available reports do not establish the exact distance between the aircraft when the alert occurred.

    TCAS is an important layer of aviation safety, particularly when aircraft encounter potentially conflicting traffic in busy airspace. The technology uses information transmitted by nearby aircraft transponders to identify potential collision threats. Depending on the circumstances, the system can problem traffic advisories or resolution advisories, recommending that pilots climb or descend to increase vertical separation.

    Industry observers note that unlike instructions from air traffic controllers, TCAS resolution advisories are generated automatically using onboard surveillance equipment. According to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual, pilots are expected to follow an RA promptly unless doing so would jeopardize the aircraft's safety. However, the circumstances surrounding the Cessna's reported lack of response remain unclear. AeroSillage noted that the available reporting does not establish whether the smaller aircraft failed to answer a radio communication or did not comply with an air traffic controller's instruction. Its registration, the nature of the communication attempts, and the minimum separation between the aircraft have not been disclosed.

    Despite the reported encounter, AC1769 continued its journey to Canada without an emergency diversion. AIRLIVE reported that the aircraft landed at Vancouver International Airport at 4:45 PM local time, completing the approximately two-hour-and-40-minute journey. Flight-tracking information independently confirms that this 737 MAX 8 operated the Palm Springs-Vancouver service and reached its destination. No other details or further emergency involving the aircraft were reported. Nevertheless, the incident illustrates how unexpected traffic conflicts can require immediate action even during otherwise routine departures.

    It has been revealed that based on available reporting, no specific findings from the US or Canadian authorities have established the circumstances of the encounter. Without an official reconstruction, it remains impossible to determine whether the Cessna experienced a communication problem, whether an instruction was missed, or how close the aircraft actually came.

    #134128. Why JSX Just Bought Newly introduced Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)

    Why JSX Just Bought Newly introduced Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired Latest Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.
    • If you’re not familiar with Fresh Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.
    • JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired Latest Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

    If you’re not familiar with Fresh Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

    Let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

    It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

    Then there’s New Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business plan was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

    The business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

    That brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

    JSX acquires Fresh Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy.

    On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. Latest Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

    According to recent reports, long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a manufacturer that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

    In a recent development, going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

    Industry observers note that under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

    According to recent reports, I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with New Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

    If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

    JSX has just bought Latest Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

    It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have plans to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

    What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

    #134126. Tech Report: What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1006 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov.
    • The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • Industry observers note that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

    The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    Industry observers note that however, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    Recent findings suggest that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Sources indicate that black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They demonstrated up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    According to recent reports, keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson strategy?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    It has been revealed that scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she mentioned.

    In a recent development, colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    Amex Blue Cash Preferred Review: A Top Cash Back Card For Everyday Purchases

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that if you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat.
    • In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.
    • Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that if you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat. The card offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets and on select streaming subscriptions, which can add up fast for families and anyone with a few monthly subscriptions.

    In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.

    Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express.

    Before I get into the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card review, here’s a quick look at the most crucial features and fees:.

    And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:.

    When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

    In a recent development, the Amex Blue Cash Preferred is at the moment offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    That’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

    Amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:.

    As you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards. No first year annual fee is a nice perk, as it lets you test the card and see how much value you’re getting before you commit to the ongoing fee.

    If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

    You can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost, so that their spending can help you rack up rewards.

    It has been revealed that I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

    Sources indicate that this is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

    It has been revealed that to put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

    Note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

    It has been revealed that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

    If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

    Industry observers note that for purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

    With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Recent findings suggest that as is the case for any credit card, it’s also crucial to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee….

    It has been revealed that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required).

    Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

    Enjoy 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 12 months from the date of account opening. After that, your APR will be a variable APR of 19.74% - 28.74%.

    This could be helpful if you need to transfer an existing credit card balance and have some time to pay it off before interest kicks in, or if you need some extra time to pay off a significant upcoming purchase. Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

    Industry observers note that one benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

    Different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    In a recent development, car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Manufacturer. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card offers the following benefits when you shop with the card:.

    In a recent development, these are all helpful benefits that you hopefully won’t have to use (though they do provide some peace of mind). Just remember you need to purchase the relevant items with your card to get this coverage.

    Purchase Protection is an embedded benefit of your Card Membership and requires no enrollment. It can help protect Covered Purchases made on your Eligible Card when they’re accidentally damaged, stolen, or lost, for up to 90 days from the Covered Purchase date. The coverage is limited to up to $10,000 per occurrence, up to $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Coverage Limits Apply. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. When an American Express® Card Member charges a Covered Purchase to an Eligible Card, Extended Warranty§ can provide up to one extra year added to the Original Manufacturer’s Warranty. Applies to warranties of five (5) years or less. Coverage is up to the actual amount charged to your Card for the item up to a maximum of $10,000; not to exceed $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

    It has been revealed that I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

    If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

    The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up quickly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

    However, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

    So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

    If you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your fresh Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:.

    In my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

    The Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

    The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

    If you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

    If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:.

    In a recent development, the Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

    Recent findings suggest that the Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

    One final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

    Here’s a look at how they compare:.

    It has been revealed that the Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a substantial part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

    Recent findings suggest that the annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

    Just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.

    American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.
    • The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations.
    • In a recent development, according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A upcoming deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    In a recent development, according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The fresh lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper stated.

    It has been revealed that the airline looks to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano mentioned in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    The Aircraft Set To Replace British Airways’ Boeing 777-200ERs At London Heathrow

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, british Airways (BA) is about to retire the aircraft that built its long-haul network, but it has not told anyone exactly what will take its place at London Heathrow (LHR).
    • It has been revealed that so what is actually coming for Heathrow’s 777-200ERs?
    • Industry observers note that gatwick (LGW) is the easiest part of the puzzle to understand because BA has actually given it a delivery date.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, british Airways (BA) is about to retire the aircraft that built its long-haul network, but it has not told anyone exactly what will take its place at London Heathrow (LHR). The airline’s 43 Boeing 777-200ERs average roughly 26 years of age, according to Aerospace Global News, and most of them fly from Heathrow rather than Gatwick. The one firm date BA has given belongs to the other London airport: in a February 27, 2026 message to colleagues, CEO Sean Doyle said the first new Boeing 787-10 will be delivered to Gatwick in 2029, as published by the British Airways Media Centre.

    It has been revealed that so what is actually coming for Heathrow’s 777-200ERs? Two types dominate the picture: the Airbus A350-1000, which is already stepping onto some of that flying, and the Boeing 787-10, with the long-delayed Boeing 777-9 expected to follow. One caveat before going further. BA has published neither a retirement date nor a route-by-route replacement blueprint for Heathrow, so every swap beyond Nashville described below is a possibility. The first real clue, though, arrived from the home of country music, and it hints at a bigger shift than a simple like-for-like swap. Read on, because the answer may change which jet you board on your next transatlantic trip.

    Industry observers note that gatwick (LGW) is the easiest part of the puzzle to understand because BA has actually given it a delivery date. Aerospace Global News, citing Cirium data, reported that BA served 13 destinations from Gatwick in March 2026, all lower-yielding leisure flights, from Antigua and Cancun to Orlando and Mauritius, plus Accra and Islamabad for visiting-friends-and-relatives traffic. The same outlet notes that around 12 aircraft are typically based there and that some suggest 17 could be once the 787-10 arrives. The fresh jets are not expected to have a First cabin. The outlet also suggests that a larger Gatwick presence could make the airport more attractive to oneworld partner airlines hoping to feed connecting passengers into BA’s network.

    Recent findings suggest that there is also a technical twist. According to Turning Left For Less, BA’s earliest 787-10s lacked crew rest bunks and were range-limited, so the newly ordered aircraft will get an increased-gross-weight modification and bunks. The site lists Vancouver, Phoenix, Mauritius, Cancun and Las Vegas as routes that become workable. BA's newly ordered Boeing 787-10s will be powered by General Electric GEnx engines, following the airline's decision to introduce a second engine supplier alongside Rolls-Royce on its Dreamliner fleet. Doyle’s own message confirmed the bunks, and Aerospace Global News adds that the rest areas should be welcome news for crew, since the airline’s initial 787-10s do not have them.

    Recent findings suggest that that gives BA a relatively clean renewal path at LGW. Heathrow is harder. Most of the 43 777-200ERs are still tied to the airport, and replacing a four-class, business-heavy aircraft with a 787-10 without First would change the product as well as the capacity. Yet one Heathrow route has already provided a much more interesting clue.

    The Airbus A350-1000 is not merely a future possibility at Heathrow. As reported by Simple Flying, BA scheduled the A350-1000 to replace the 777-200ER on its daily Heathrow–Nashville service from March 29, based on schedule data first spotted by Ishrion Aviation. Published flight times stay at 9 hours 10 minutes outbound as BA223 and 8 hours 10 minutes back as BA222, although the A350 cruises slightly faster than the 777. In winter, the route has used the Boeing 787-8, and the report says there is no word yet on whether that aircraft returns once the cold season arrives.

    Simple Flying's database reveals the Heathrow 777-200ER on this route seats 272 passengers, while the A350-1000 seats 331, a jump of 59. The seat models are the same, but Simple Flying notes BA fits a smaller galley area to squeeze in the extra rows, and Turning Left For Less claims cabin crew have voiced concern about galley space on the type.

    Seat counts on Heathrow–Nashville, per aeroLOPA data cited by Simple Flying.

    Sources indicate that economy passengers may even gain a little comfort, since the A350 has one fewer seat per row than the 777. But the strategic point is bigger: BA added 59 seats to a route without adding a single flight. Why would an airline do that, and what does it say about the rest of Heathrow’s fleet? There is also a cargo angle. Simple Flying points out that the A350-1000 is comparable in size to the Boeing 777-300ER and so has a significantly larger hold, which on a short transatlantic sector lets BA load more freight than before.

    Because Heathrow is the one airport where BA cannot simply add flights. Writing in 2023, when the airline was still weighing its options, One Mile At A Time argued that Heathrow is capacity-controlled and that the larger A350-1000 and 787–10 variants offer excellent economics. They also noted that BA’s 777 fleet averaged nearly 20 years of age at the time, with nearly two-thirds of the jets delivered in 2001 or earlier, mostly the 777-200ER variant. Aerospace Global News makes a similar point about Gatwick: basing latest jets there relieves pressure on a heavily slot-constrained Heathrow hub.

    Efficiency is the other half of the logic. According to Airbus, the A350 Family delivers a 25% advantage in fuel burn, operating costs and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation competitor aircraft. That improvement comes from combining advanced aerodynamics, new-generation Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and lightweight materials, which account for more than 70% of the airframe. For BA, this makes the A350-1000 particularly attractive at a slot-constrained airport such as Heathrow: it can carry more passengers on an existing departure while benefiting from the efficiency gains of a newer-generation design.

    That combination of capacity and efficiency helps explain why BA has ordered more than one type of upcoming-generation widebody rather than choosing a single replacement for every 777. The order book tells the story. BA has 24 Boeing 777-9s on order after adding six aircraft in March 2025. It has also ordered six additional A350-1000s and 38 Boeing 787-10s, including the 32-aircraft order announced in 2025.

    Industry observers note that those numbers make one aircraft particularly important. Twenty-four 777-9s are supposed to become BA's largest upcoming-generation widebodies, but none has yet joined the fleet. The timing of that arrival could determine how quickly the oldest Heathrow 777s can finally disappear.

    In a recent development, the 777-9 is the biggest aircraft in BA's replacement plan, and it is also the one that introduces the most uncertainty. We reported in August 2026 that the aircraft was still working through the tail end of its certification sequence as of mid-2026. In a November piece, we added that Boeing is expected to deliver its first 777-9 in 2027, by which time Airbus will likely have well over 150 A350-1000s flying.

    For BA, Turning Left For Less expects a four-class layout of eight First, 65 Club Suites, 46 World Traveller Plus and 206 economy seats, 325 in all, debuting from 2027 or 2028 with the airline’s latest First suite. Against the A350-1000’s 331 seats, the 777-9 would not even add capacity on a Nashville-type route, which complicates the idea of the 777-9 as a simple 777-200ER successor.

    The same site expects the new First suite to be limited to the 24 Boeing 777-9s and the 12 refurbished Airbus A380s, which would make the 777-9 as much a flagship statement as a fleet-replacement tool.

    Until the 777-9 demonstrates up, the old jets keep flying, and flying hard, with most replacements still years away. What does that wait mean for passengers boarding one tomorrow?

    According to recent reports, that leaves BA with an awkward transition period. Turning Left For Less indicates BA intends to retire all 43 777-200ERs, some of which will exceed 30 years of age by withdrawal, and its reader analysis suggests the last four, delivered in 2009, could stay longer because they are younger. BA has confirmed none of that beyond Doyle’s statement about Gatwick. Put differently, the exit date for the oldest airframes is still a matter of informed speculation, not a published schedule.

    It has been revealed that the wait has had visible moments. FlyMag reported that BA229 to Baltimore returned to Heathrow on July 9, 2026, and BA183 to New York turned back the next evening, both operated by 777-200ERs after crews identified technical issues, and both flights were subsequently canceled. Age alone is not proof of unreliability, since many 777s worldwide have flown happily for decades, but the incidents landed just as the renewal timeline moved into focus.

    Industry observers note that every extra month of waiting sharpens the question BA has so far left unanswered in public: which Heathrow route loses its 777-200ER next, and will passengers on it get a First cabin back? The answer may arrive route by route, in schedule filings, long before any formal announcement.

    It has been revealed that two milestones will settle how this plays out, and neither is fully in BA’s hands. The first is the pace of 787-10 deliveries after the Gatwick debut in 2029. The second is whether Boeing can certify and hand over the 777-9 on the schedule it now promises. If the Dreamliners flow, BA can retire 777-200ERs without leaving Heathrow gaps. If the 777-9 slips again, the A350-1000 is the obvious stopgap, yet the six additional aircraft on order are a modest cushion.

    According to recent reports, there is a premium-cabin cost to watch as well. Turning Left For Less points out that the new First suite does not fit four abreast in a 787 and that the A350-1000 carries no First at all, so some Heathrow routes could lose the cabin entirely as the 777-200ERs go. That is precisely the trade-off BA has not yet explained to the customers paying for it. Some will welcome newer jets with quieter cabins and more consistent Club Suites; others will see a quiet downgrade of the flagship experience at the airport where BA charges its highest fares.

    Recent findings suggest that one Mile At A Time wrote a 2023 article saying they were curious about how it would all play out. Three years on, the cast is clear, but the final act is not. So what do you think: should BA hold on to its youngest 777-200ERs until the 777-9 arrives, or are the A350-1000 and 787-10 enough on their own? Tell us in the comments, and let us know which Heathrow route you would like to see upgraded first.
